label: sec:exp-pre-reduce
title: Reducing exp-Instances
html:
Every translated TPBV​-formula contains exp(2,k) for the width k of its operations. In several cases, the translation also creates other instances whose exponents differ from k by a constant. Signed operations, such as signed comparisons and sign extensions, test the most significant bit and thus add exp(2,k−1), and in multi-width formulas, widths that differ by a constant c add exp(2,k−c). The solver treats every distinct exp-instance as a separate term, which the CEGAR-style loop must refine on its own, although all of these instances are related. The pass of this section reduces the number of distinct exp-instances in the translated formula.

Within each group of same-base powers whose exponents differ by a numeral, every power is expressed via the power with the smallest exponent, i.e., exp(b,e+c)→bc⋅exp(b,e), so that only one exp-instance per group remains. The rule is only applied if e≥0 is entailed. Without this guard, it is unsound, e.g., exp(2,−1+1)=1 but 2⋅exp(2,−1)=0. Unlike division, multiplication keeps the divisibility of exp(b,e+c) by bc syntactic. This choice solves the most benchmarks, compared to taking the most frequent or the largest exponent as the representative (Appendix C).

Extended: Appendix C. Reducing Exponentiation Instances

Table 14 compares three choices of the representative for the reduction of exp-instances of Section 4.4, all under the guard of Section 4.4 on the smaller exponent of each pair. We run this evaluation with configuration cvc5 of Table 9. Row – is the baseline without reducing exp-instances. Choice div takes the power with the largest exponent, with every other power expressed by division (exp(b,e)→exp(b,e+c)divbc, which additionally requires b=0). Choice common takes the power whose exponent occurs most often, with larger powers expressed by multiplication and smaller ones by division. Choice mul takes the power with the smallest exponent, with every other power expressed by multiplication (exp(b,e+c)→bc⋅exp(b,e)). Every choice of reducing exp-instances improves on the baseline. Choice mul solves the most benchmarks and is used in the rest of the paper.
